meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I always swing at the ball with all my might. I hit or miss big'?
meta.ogDescription: Babe Ruth, in a 1920 newspaper piece. The full sentence is stranger and better than the fragment people quote.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ places this in a newspaper article of 13 August 1920 — “Keep Your Eye On the Ball”, written by Ruth as told to the sportswriter Westbrook Pegler ↗ , and running in the Chicago Tribune of that date at p. 11. Pegler was then a sports writer for United News; he did not join the Tribune until 1925, so the piece most likely reached it by syndication — that last step is our inference, not something either source states. That is a specific, checkable citation, and we could not check it: the newspaper’s own archive refuses us. We say “attributed” because we have not read the page, not because anything suggests it is wrong.

source.heading: The sentence people stop quoting halfway

Not independently confirmed — both cited archives are closed to us

source.excerpt: I always swing at the ball with all my might. I hit or miss big and when I miss I know it long before the umpire calls a strike on me, for every muscle in my back, shoulders and arms is groaning, “You missed it.” And believe me, it is no fun to miss a ball that hard. Once I put myself out of the game for a few days by a miss like that.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists this in its sourced section with a full citation: “Keep Your Eye On the Ball”, by Ruth as told to Pegler, Chicago Tribune, 13 August 1920, p. 11, reprinted in Playing the Game: My Early Years in Baseball, p. 29.

We tried both and failed. The Chicago Tribune’s archive returns HTTP 403 to us, and the Google Books copy of the reprint serves no readable text. Neither link is cited here as corroboration, because we cannot say what it contains.

We also checked where it is not. The line does not appear in the full text of Ruth’s 1928 book ↗, and a Library of Congress newspaper search for two distinctive phrases from the passage returned nothing — that collection does not hold the 1920 Tribune.
source.excerptNote: This is Wikiquote’s transcription of the 1920 article, not our reading of the original — we could not open it. Worth noting how much the popular fragment leaves out: the interesting half is Ruth describing what a miss feels like in the muscles of his back.

author.name: Babe Ruth
author.heading: About Babe Ruth
author.bio: George Herman “Babe” Ruth spent 22 seasons in Major League Baseball, beginning as a left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox and becoming, with the New York Yankees, the player who reorganised the sport around the home run. In 1920, his first Yankees season, he hit 54 home runs and led the league in strikeouts — the trade-off this sentence describes.

context.heading: Hitting or missing big
lead: In 1920, his first season with the Yankees, Ruth hit fifty-four home runs — more than any other team in the American League except one. He also led the league in strikeouts. The two facts are the same fact, and this sentence is him saying so, in August of that season, while it was happening.

The all-or-nothing swing was a genuine tactical argument at the time, not a slogan. Ruth was proposing that the strikeouts were worth it. The rest of baseball spent the next century agreeing with him.
